set.st: About 1874 a Jackson prison convict told Ottawa County coroner Curtis W. Gray he had buried several thousand dollars of robbery gold 'in the hill immediately back of the light house', beside a described tree on Light House Hill. Gray and Marshal Ike Sanford dug and found nothing. In October 1899 N. Stebbins and Col. William C. Baty of Pueblo, Colorado, searched the hill with 'metal instruments'; five days later the Tribune wrote that 'many persons in town believe that Col. Baty the treasure hunter found the gold he was searching after.' In April 1900 Baty returned with a Mr. Robinson and two labourers and sank a planked shaft from the crest of Five Mile Hill, the big dune south of the harbour; after three weeks, a 90-ft hole and 3,000 ft of lumber in the curbing, he quit on 7 May 1900 with nothing, and the hole was to be filled. Pin is the crest of the hill, not a cache spot. The Grand Rapids Herald's fuller telling (1900): some forty years earlier officer Curtis W. Gray took a dying Jackson prisoner's confession that a gang had made a big bank haul, fled to the mouth of the Grand and split the loot. The man carried his share, 'mostly gold and diamonds', at dawn to 'the place where the light house stands, then turned into the woods' and buried it 'on the top of a little ridge of sandy soil … near the light house, overlooking the lake and river', drawing a chart; Gray dug shallow holes and found nothing. Baty, 'a mine owner and prospector', dug at 'the summit of the Five Mile hill' in 1899; in April 1900 he and his partner Robinson hired diggers at $1 a foot, reached 20 ft aiming for 60, and turned up a page of an 1879 Grand Rapids Eagle at about 20 ft. By 25-30 Apr the shaft was about 70 ft deep, reached by rope, and hundreds of people visited it; no find was reported. The spot was 'just back of the summit', reached by the river ridge through the woods. A 1903 wire gave the fullest version: the dying Jackson convict told Gray (called the county sheriff there; he was coroner) that loot from 'a sensational robbery in Kalamazoo', about $40,000 in gold coin and diamonds in two satchels, had been carried up the shore from Saugatuck by two crooks and buried near Five-Mile Hill, 'in the lake shore sands within the city limits of Grand Haven'. Gray searched without success, then told friends, and parties hunted 'year after year'. A 1913 Detroit Free Press feature names the convict as William Jenkins, jailed by Gray for horse stealing in Civil War days and later given life at Joliet for a bank robbery. Dying of tuberculosis, he told Gray that he and two others had brought $30,000 in gold from a western bank job by way of Milwaukee and buried it at the base of Five-Mile Hill between two pines, and he drew a map. Lumbermen cut the pines, and Gray dug for weeks. The feature calls Baty 'Ichabod Beattie', a Pueblo miner with a metal 'indicator', and says his shaft went 95 ft. Later seekers included James O'Connell and John Luiken, and in 1921 the Tribune said someone dug into the hill 'every decade'. A Tribune item of 18 Apr 1900 names Baty's partner as J. R. Robinson, also of Pueblo. By 1932 the city's water storage tanks stood on Five Mile Hill. No later find was reported. The Grand Rapids Press (11 Oct 1899) put Baty's first dig 'at the very pinnacle of Five Mile Hill', 'back of the lighthouse', with a team and scraper down 12-15 ft and aiming for 30-40 ft, guided by a $125 'instrument'; it said the pot was 'said to be worth $60,000'. It was remembered locally in a 1916 school essay, 'The Treasure in the Five Mile Hill' (not printed), and a 1920 twenty-years-ago Tribune column; still no find.
